title: High-dimensional quantum process tomography with undetected photons
abstract: The goal of quantum process tomography is to fully characterize an operation performed on a quantum state. By considering high-dimensional quantum states (qudit), we show that it is possible to fully reconstruct an arbitrary operation without performing any measurement on the transformed qudit. Our method is interferometric and conceptually different from existing techniques of quantum process tomography that must perform a measurement on the transformed qudit.
summary: The paper presents a novel Quantum Process Tomography technique for high-dimensional qudits using photons. Instead of measuring the output state directly, it reconstructs an unknown process by analyzing interference patterns generated between two paths. This method is powerful because it allows full characterization without performing any measurement on the photon acted upon by the unknown operator.
main_problem: The goal is to fully characterize an arbitrary linear quantum operation ($\mathcal{E}$) acting on a high-dimensional photonic qudit without performing any direct measurement on the output state.
main_result: A method is proposed that reconstructs all matrix elements of the unknown process $\mathbf{b}_T$ by measuring single-photon interference patterns generated through an auxiliary, known unitary transformation ($\mathbf{b}_U$).
method: The reconstruction relies on analyzing the sinusoidal variation of the single-photon detection probability ($P_d$) as a function of a tunable interferometric phase ($\varphi_{in}$). By systematically varying $\mathbf{b}_U$, all necessary information about $\mathbf{b}_T$ can be extracted.
model_or_system: The system uses photonic qudits encoded in Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM) states. The process involves an unknown non-unitary operator ($\mathbf{b}_T$) acting on one photon path, while a known unitary operator ($\mathbf{b}_U$) acts on another, allowing for interference measurements.
key_observables: Single-photon detection probability ($P_d$), visibility ($V$), and the phase shifts observed in the interference patterns.
important_parameters: The dimensionality $N$ of the qudit space; the tunable interferometric phase $\varphi_{in}$.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that quantum interference by path identity makes which-path information unavailable for the signal photon, and it relies on specific field operator transformations to handle non-unitary operations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the general QPT scheme using a Zou-Wang-Mandel interferometer. Figure 2 demonstrates the retrieval of specific matrix elements ($T_{11}, T_{23}, T_{31}$) by analyzing interference patterns and visibilities.
paper_structure: The paper first defines the problem in high dimensions, details the interferometric setup using two sources and path splitting, derives the dependence of $P_d$ on phases (Chunk 1), and then systematically outlines a protocol to determine all matrix elements by varying $\mathbf{b}_U$ pairs (Chunk 2).
why_interesting: This work provides an elegant measurement-free characterization technique for quantum channels, which is crucial for validating complex photonic quantum hardware where destructive measurements are undesirable or impossible.

Idler beam, I1, is sent through Q2 and perfectly aligned with idler beam I2. This alignment induces coherence between signal beams S1 and S2. Consequently, a single-photon interference pattern is created when S1 and S2 are superposed by a beamsplit- ter (BS2) and one of the outputs is detected after projecting the signal photon onto a chosen mode.
